title: Organic Chemistry Laboratory
description: The practical side of organic chemistry: lab safety and notebooks, glassware, workup and purification techniques, and the standard experiments with their reactions, procedures, characterization and common problems.

entries.name: Safety, lab notebooks and reports
entries.tagline: How to work safely, record what you do, and report it.

points: Splash-proof goggles at all times, a lab coat, long trousers and closed shoes. Tie back long hair.
Read the safety data sheet (SDS) for every chemical before using it, and know its hazards from the pictograms (flammable, corrosive, toxic, oxidizer, health hazard, environmental hazard).
Work with volatile, toxic or smelly chemicals in a fume hood, with the sash low.
Keep flammable solvents (ether, hexane, acetone, ethanol) away from flames and hot surfaces. Use hot plates, heating mantles or baths, not open flames. Never heat a closed system.
Gloves: nitrile gloves protect against many chemicals but dichloromethane and ethers go through them in seconds, so change them when splashed.
Know where the eyewash, safety shower, fire extinguisher, fire blanket and exits are. For an eye splash, rinse for 15 minutes. Never work alone, and never eat, drink or pipette by mouth.
Separate waste into labeled containers: halogenated organic (dichloromethane, chloroform), non-halogenated organic, aqueous (acid, base, heavy metals separately), solid waste and broken glass.
Never pour organic solvents or heavy-metal solutions down the drain. Quench reactive reagents (hydrides, Grignards, sodium) before disposal.
Bound pages, ink, dated and numbered. Never erase or tear out. Cross out an error with a single line.

Before the lab: the purpose, the balanced reaction, a table of reagents with molar mass, amount (mass and mmol), equivalents, melting or boiling point, density and hazards, and the procedure in your own words.
During: record what you actually do, with amounts to the precision measured, times, temperatures and observations (color changes, gas, precipitate).
After: the yield, percent yield, melting point (as a range), spectra and their interpretation, and conclusions.

sections.text: Find the limiting reagent, calculate the theoretical yield in grams from the stoichiometry, then percent yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100%. A yield above 100% means the product is wet or impure, not that more was made than possible.
Abstract, introduction and reaction scheme, procedure, results (with the data in tables), discussion of the yield, purity and sources of error, answers to questions, and references.

quiz.q: Which waste container should dichloromethane go into?
quiz.a: Halogenated organic waste

quiz.q: A yield above 100% most likely means…
quiz.a: The product is wet or impure
wrong: The theoretical yield is wrong by definition

entries.name: Glassware and setting up reactions
entries.tagline: The pieces of an organic lab, and how to assemble them safely.

facts: For heating and reflux. Rounded to spread stress, so it can take heat and vacuum. Needs a cork ring or clamp to stand.
For storing, swirling and recrystallization. Never for vacuum, except a thick-walled filter flask.
Ground glass joints (such as 14/20, 19/22 or 24/40), which fit any equal-size part. Grease lightly or use PTFE sleeves, and secure with Keck clips.
Water enters at the bottom and leaves at the top so the jacket stays full.
For adding a reagent dropwise to control an exothermic reaction. The pressure-equalizing version lets the liquid flow in a closed system.
Collects water from a refluxing mixture (often with toluene) to drive a reaction forward.
Filled with CaCl₂ to keep moisture out of a reaction that is open to the air.
For vacuum filtration. Hirsch for small amounts.

points: Clamp everything to a rack, stable and plumb. The apparatus must never be completely closed when heated.

Heating: heating mantle, oil bath, sand bath or hot plate with an aluminum block. A magnetic stir bar gives even heating. Boiling chips (not under vacuum, and not added to hot liquid) are the alternative.
Fill the flask only between one third and two thirds.
Inspect glassware for star-shaped cracks, especially before vacuum or heating.

sections.text: For air- or moisture-sensitive reagents, flame- or oven-dry the glassware, assemble it hot, and flush with nitrogen or argon, with a balloon or a gas line and bubbler.

quiz.q: In a water-cooled condenser, where does the cooling water enter?
quiz.a: At the bottom

entries.name: Workup and drying agents
entries.tagline: Turning a reaction mixture into a crude product, step by step.

points: Quench: stop the reaction, for example by adding water, dilute acid, ammonium chloride, or by cooling.

Extract the product into an organic solvent (diethyl ether, ethyl acetate or dichloromethane) in a separatory funnel. Keep both layers until the product is safely isolated, as you may have the wrong one.

Wash the organic layer. Water removes polar impurities and salts. Saturated sodium bicarbonate removes acids (vent, because CO₂ forms). Dilute HCl removes amines. Dilute NaOH removes phenols and carboxylic acids. Each wash moves an impurity into the aqueous layer.
Brine (saturated NaCl) is the last wash. It pulls much of the dissolved water out of the organic layer and helps break emulsions.
Dry with an anhydrous salt, filter or decant it off, and remove the solvent.

facts: High capacity, neutral, slow and not very efficient. Add until some powder moves freely, like a snow globe, and not in clumps.
Fast and efficient, fine powder, very slightly acidic.
Good for hydrocarbons and alkyl halides, but reacts with alcohols, amines and carbonyls.

sections.text: A flask is rotated in a warm water bath (about 40 °C) under reduced pressure, which spreads a film of liquid on the glass so the solvent evaporates quickly and gently. Use a bump trap, and do not fill the flask more than half. Take care not to lose a volatile product.

points: Emulsion: a cloudy layer that will not separate. Add brine, wait, swirl gently, or filter through Celite.
Can't tell which layer is which: add a drop of water and see where it goes. Density is a guide but concentrated solutions can change it.

quiz.q: Why is brine used as the last wash?
quiz.a: It pulls water out of the organic layer and helps break emulsions

entries.name: Thin-layer chromatography in practice
entries.tagline: The quickest way to see how a reaction is going and whether a product is pure.

points: Use a silica gel plate with a fluorescent indicator (F₂₅₄). Draw a pencil line about 1 cm from the bottom, never ink, which would run.
Spot small amounts with a fine capillary, in separate lanes. Keep spots small.
Place in a covered chamber with the solvent about 0.5 cm deep, below the line. Let it rise until it is about 1 cm from the top. Mark the solvent front with a pencil at once, and dry.
Calculate Rf = distance of the spot ÷ distance of the solvent front.

sections.text: Run three lanes: starting material, reaction mixture and a co-spot of both. The co-spot confirms which spot is which. A finished reaction shows no starting material spot.

points: Mixtures of hexanes and ethyl acetate, from 9:1 for nonpolar compounds to 1:1 for polar ones, are the usual choice.
Aim for an Rf of 0.2–0.5. A more polar solvent moves all spots higher.
Polar compounds, such as alcohols and acids, move less. Acids can streak, which a drop of acetic acid in the solvent reduces. Amines streak, which triethylamine reduces.

facts: Conjugated and aromatic compounds quench the fluorescence and appear as dark spots. Non-destructive, so do it first.
Many organic compounds take up iodine and turn brown. Reversible.
Oxidizable compounds (alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes) appear yellow on a purple background.
A wide range of colors, good for many functional groups.
Amines and amino acids give purple.

quiz.q: Why is a pencil used, not a pen, to mark a TLC plate?
quiz.a: Ink would dissolve and run in the solvent
wrong: Pencil is more visible under UV

entries.name: Column chromatography in practice
entries.tagline: How to pack, load and run a silica column to purify a product.

points: Use TLC to find a solvent in which the desired product has an Rf of about 0.25–0.35, and which separates it from impurities by at least 0.15 in Rf.
Use about 30–100 times as much silica (by mass) as sample. More for harder separations.
Plug the tube with cotton or glass wool and add a layer of sand. Fill with a slurry of silica in the starting solvent (wet packing), tapping to remove bubbles. Add sand on top to protect the surface.
Never let the solvent level fall below the top of the silica, or the column will crack and the separation is ruined.

Load the sample in the smallest possible volume of solvent. For samples that dissolve poorly, dry load by dissolving in a volatile solvent, adding some silica, evaporating, and putting the powder on top.
Push solvent through with gentle air or nitrogen pressure (flash chromatography), about 2 inches per minute of solvent drop.
Collect fractions of equal volume in test tubes, and check them by TLC.
Start with a less polar solvent and, if needed, move stepwise to a more polar one (gradient). Less polar compounds come out first.
Combine pure fractions and evaporate the solvent.

sections.text: Cracks or bubbles in the silica, a band that is too wide because the sample was loaded in too much solvent, overloading, and compounds that decompose on acidic silica (add a little triethylamine or use alumina).

quiz.q: What is a good Rf for the desired compound on the TLC before running a column?

entries.name: Distillation techniques in practice
entries.tagline: Simple, fractional, vacuum and steam distillation: when to use each, and how to do it well.

points: Place the thermometer bulb just below the side arm of the still head, so it measures the temperature of the vapor entering the condenser. The reading is the boiling point of the distilling liquid.
Fill the flask one third to two thirds, add a stir bar or boiling chips, and heat gradually. Aim for a steady rate of about one drop per second.
Collect a forerun (the first few drops, with low-boiling impurities), then the main fraction while the temperature is steady. Change the receiver if the temperature rises sharply.
Never distill to dryness. Residues may be unstable, and ethers can contain explosive peroxides.
For liquids with boiling points closer than about 25–70 °C, add a fractionating column, packed with steel wool or glass beads, and keep it insulated.

sections.text: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, which suits high-boiling or heat-sensitive compounds. A nomograph converts a boiling point between pressures. As a rule of thumb, reducing the pressure from 760 to about 20 mmHg lowers the boiling point by about 100–150 °C. Use a stir bar (boiling chips do not work under vacuum), a Claisen adapter, check the glass for cracks, and put a trap between the apparatus and the pump. Release the vacuum before turning off the heat.

For compounds that do not mix with water and are sensitive to heat, steam is passed through the sample (or it is boiled with water). The total vapor pressure is the sum of the water's and the compound's, so the mixture boils below 100 °C and the compound comes over with the water. It is used for natural products such as limonene from orange peel and eugenol from cloves. The product is then extracted from the distillate.
The Kugelrohr (bulb-to-bulb distillation) uses a series of glass bulbs in an oven under vacuum, for milligram to gram amounts.

quiz.q: Where should the thermometer bulb be in a simple distillation?
quiz.a: Just below the side arm of the still head
wrong: At the top of the condenser

quiz.q: Why does steam distillation work for compounds immiscible with water?
quiz.a: The vapor pressures add, so the mixture boils below 100 °C

entries.name: Recrystallization, sublimation and melting points in practice
entries.tagline: Purifying a solid and checking the result.

points: Test solvents on a few milligrams: the solid should dissolve poorly in the cold solvent and easily when hot. Ethanol, water, ethyl acetate, hexanes and toluene are common, and mixtures too.
Dissolve the solid in the minimum amount of boiling solvent, added in portions. Using too much solvent is the usual cause of a low yield.
Colored impurities: add a pinch of activated carbon to the hot solution, and filter. Too much carbon adsorbs the product.
Insoluble impurities: filter the hot solution through fluted filter paper in a pre-warmed funnel, keeping everything hot so that the product does not crystallize in the funnel (hot filtration).
Cool slowly to room temperature, then in ice. Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals. If none form, scratch the flask with a glass rod or add a seed crystal.
Collect by vacuum filtration and wash with a small amount of ice-cold solvent. Dry.

sections.text: Dissolve in the minimum hot amount of the good solvent (such as ethanol), then add the poor solvent (water) dropwise until the solution just turns cloudy, add a drop of the good solvent to clear it, and cool.

If the product separates as an oil, the melting point of the product (lowered by impurities) is below the temperature of the solution. Reheat, add more solvent, and cool more slowly or use a lower-boiling solvent.

Some solids, such as caffeine, camphor and ferrocene, go directly from solid to vapor when heated, and re-form as crystals on a cold surface. A cold-finger sublimator, under vacuum, separates them from non-volatile impurities without any solvent.

points: Pack 2–3 mm of dry, powdered solid in a capillary tube. Heat quickly to find the approximate melting point, then repeat slowly, about 1–2 °C per minute near the melting point.
Record the range from the first liquid to the last solid. A pure compound melts within about 1–2 °C, and impurities lower and widen the range.
Typical values: naphthalene 80 °C, benzoic acid 122 °C, acetanilide 114 °C, urea 133 °C, aspirin 135 °C, biphenyl 69 °C.

quiz.q: Your product separates as an oil on cooling. What should you do?
quiz.a: Reheat, add more solvent, and cool more slowly
wrong: Cool it in dry ice at once

entries.name: Spectroscopy in the organic lab: NMR, IR and GC
terms: GC analysis of a reaction mixture
entries.tagline: Preparing samples and avoiding the traps of reading your spectra.

points: Dissolve 5–20 mg (for ¹H) in about 0.6–0.7 mL of a deuterated solvent, usually CDCl₃, in a clean, dry NMR tube. The liquid should be 4–5 cm deep. Filter out any solid, which spoils the lineshape.
The residual CHCl₃ in CDCl₃ appears at 7.26 ppm (¹³C at 77.2 ppm as a triplet). Water in CDCl₃ appears near 1.56 ppm.
Integrate to find the ratio of hydrogens, and the ratio of two compounds in a mixture (for example the ratio of products).

sections.text: A product that still contains solvent shows up here, and it is a common reason for a yield above 100%.

points: Neat liquid: a drop pressed between two salt plates (NaCl or KBr). Never touch the plates with wet hands or water, which dissolve them.
ATR: place the sample directly on the crystal and press. The easiest, for liquids and solids.
KBr pellet: grind about 1 mg of solid with dry KBr and press into a disc.
Look for the functional groups: O–H (broad, 3200–3600), C=O (1650–1800), C≡N (about 2250), N–O of nitro (1530 and 1350). Check also for the absence of a starting material band.

sections.text: Gas chromatography of a small sample dissolved in a volatile solvent gives the purity, and the ratio of isomers or products from the peak areas (with a correction for the detector response if needed). Lower-boiling compounds come out first on a nonpolar column.

quiz.q: Where does residual CHCl₃ appear in a ¹H NMR spectrum run in CDCl₃?
quiz.a: 7.26 ppm

entries.name: Experiment: Fischer esterification (isopentyl acetate)
entries.tagline: Making the smell of bananas, and using Le Chatelier's principle.

sections.text: The equilibrium constant is only about 4, so the reaction is pushed forward with an excess of one reagent. Here, acetic acid is cheap and used in excess.

points: Combine isopentyl alcohol (3-methyl-1-butanol), excess glacial acetic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid with a boiling chip or stir bar, and reflux for about an hour. Use a heating mantle or sand bath.
Cool, add water, and extract into diethyl ether or use the ester layer directly.
Wash with water, then with sodium bicarbonate to remove the acetic acid and the catalyst. Vent often, because CO₂ forms. Finish with brine.
Dry over anhydrous sodium sulfate or magnesium sulfate, filter, and distill (bp of isopentyl acetate 142 °C).
IR: strong C=O stretch near 1740 cm⁻¹ and C–O near 1240, and no broad O–H band (3300), which shows the alcohol and acid are gone.
¹H NMR: a triplet at about 4.1 ppm (OCH₂), a singlet at 2.05 (CH₃C=O), and a doublet at 0.9 (6H) from the isopropyl group.
Typical yield: 60–80%. The product smells of bananas.

sections.text: Use a larger excess of acid, or remove the water as it forms with a Dean–Stark trap. Losses occur in the washes and on distillation.

quiz.q: How is the yield of a Fischer esterification increased?
quiz.a: Use an excess of one reagent or remove the water

quiz.q: What IR band shows that the ester has formed?
quiz.a: A strong C=O stretch near 1740 cm⁻¹

entries.name: Experiment: Grignard synthesis (triphenylmethanol)
entries.tagline: Building a carbon–carbon bond with an organomagnesium reagent, in dry glassware.

sections.text: The alternative is methyl or ethyl benzoate with two equivalents of the Grignard reagent, which also gives triphenylmethanol.

points: Everything must be dry. Oven- or flame-dry the glassware, use anhydrous ether and a drying tube. Water destroys the Grignard reagent, giving benzene.

Place magnesium turnings in the flask, crush a few pieces to expose fresh metal, and add a little bromobenzene in ether, with a crystal of iodine if needed. The reaction starts with bubbling, cloudiness and warming. Then add the rest slowly so that the ether refluxes gently.
Add benzophenone in ether dropwise. A red or pink color appears and fades.
Quench with dilute sulfuric acid or aqueous ammonium chloride, with cooling. Separate the layers and extract with ether.

A side product is biphenyl, from coupling of the Grignard reagent with unreacted bromobenzene. It is nonpolar and is washed out of the solid by trituration with cold petroleum ether or ligroin (biphenyl mp 69 °C).
Recrystallize the triphenylmethanol (mp 161–163 °C).
IR: broad O–H near 3400 cm⁻¹, and no C=O near 1660 cm⁻¹ from benzophenone.
Typical yield: 40–70%.

sections.text: The reaction does not start (wet glassware or oxidized magnesium), and a low yield from moisture or from adding the bromobenzene too fast, which gives more biphenyl.

quiz.q: Why must the glassware be dry in a Grignard reaction?
quiz.a: Water protonates and destroys the Grignard reagent

quiz.q: What is the usual byproduct of this Grignard synthesis?
quiz.a: Biphenyl

entries.name: Experiment: nucleophilic substitution (1-bromobutane, t-butyl chloride, rates)
entries.tagline: One experiment for SN2 and one for SN1, and rate tests that tell them apart.

points: 1-Butanol is heated under reflux with sodium bromide and sulfuric acid, which makes HBr in the flask. Protonation of the OH gives a leaving group, and bromide attacks the primary carbon.

Distill the crude 1-bromobutane. Wash with water, cold concentrated sulfuric acid (removes unreacted alcohol and dibutyl ether), water and sodium bicarbonate. Dry over calcium chloride, and distill (bp 101–102 °C).
Side products: dibutyl ether, 1-butene and 2-bromobutane (small).
tert-Butanol is shaken with concentrated HCl in a separatory funnel for about 15 minutes. The tertiary carbocation forms easily and chloride adds.
Separate the upper layer, wash with water and bicarbonate (vent), dry with calcium chloride, and distill (bp 51–52 °C). It is volatile, so keep it cold.

facts: Iodide is a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent. NaCl and NaBr are not soluble in acetone, so a precipitate shows that reaction has taken place. Rates: primary > secondary ≫ tertiary. Methyl and benzylic and allylic halides are fast.
Silver ion pulls the halide off, giving a carbocation, and AgX precipitates. Rates: tertiary > secondary ≫ primary. Benzylic and allylic are fast.

sections.text: Leaving group ability: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl.

quiz.q: In the NaI/acetone test, which halide reacts fastest?
quiz.a: A primary alkyl bromide

quiz.q: Which halide reacts fastest with AgNO₃ in ethanol?
quiz.a: A tertiary alkyl halide

entries.name: Experiment: dehydration of cyclohexanol (E1)
entries.tagline: Making an alkene by acid-catalyzed elimination and distilling it out as it forms.

sections.text: Protonation of the OH, loss of water to give a secondary carbocation, and loss of a proton (E1). The reaction is an equilibrium, and the lower-boiling alkene (bp 83 °C) is distilled out as it forms, to drive it forward.

points: Heat cyclohexanol with 85% phosphoric acid (preferred to sulfuric acid, which chars and oxidizes) in a flask with a fractional distillation setup. Collect the distillate while the temperature at the head stays below about 90 °C.
Wash the distillate with saturated sodium chloride and sodium bicarbonate, to remove acid. Dry with calcium chloride or sodium sulfate, and redistill (bp 81–83 °C).
Typical yield: 50–70%.
Bromine in dichloromethane (or bromine water) loses its orange color, by addition across the C=C.
Baeyer test: dilute potassium permanganate turns from purple to brown MnO₂, by oxidation of the C=C to a diol.
IR: no broad O–H (3300), a C–H stretch above 3000 cm⁻¹ (=C–H, 3020) and a weak C=C near 1650 cm⁻¹. GC shows purity.

sections.text: Dicyclohexyl ether (from two molecules of alcohol), and polymer. Water in the distillate shows as cloudiness, and so it must be dried.

quiz.q: Why is cyclohexene distilled out as it is formed?
quiz.a: To shift the equilibrium toward the product

entries.name: Experiment: aldol condensation (dibenzalacetone)
entries.tagline: A crossed aldol condensation that gives a bright yellow solid.

sections.text: A Claisen–Schmidt condensation. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it cannot form an enolate and can only act as the electrophile. Acetone forms the enolate, and so there is little self-condensation. Each aldol step is followed by loss of water to give a conjugated enone.

points: Dissolve sodium hydroxide in water and ethanol. Add benzaldehyde and acetone (2 : 1 mole ratio) and stir at room temperature for about 15–30 minutes. A yellow solid forms.
Filter by vacuum, wash with water until the washings are neutral (to remove NaOH) and then with a little cold ethanol.
Recrystallize from ethyl acetate or ethanol (mp 110–112 °C for the trans,trans isomer). Typical yield is 70–90%.
IR: conjugated C=O near 1650 cm⁻¹, lower than that of a simple ketone (1715) because of conjugation, and C=C near 1590.
¹H NMR: two vinyl doublets, with J about 16 Hz showing trans double bonds, and aromatic signals.
UV–vis: a strong absorption near 330 nm.

sections.text: A low melting point suggests the mono-condensation product, benzalacetone (mp 42 °C), from too little benzaldehyde. Too much base or time can cause the Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde and an oily product.

quiz.q: Why does benzaldehyde not undergo self-condensation here?
quiz.a: It has no α-hydrogens to form an enolate
wrong: It is not a carbonyl compound

entries.name: Experiment: Diels–Alder reaction
entries.tagline: Two classic versions: cyclopentadiene at room temperature, and anthracene in hot xylene.

points: Cyclopentadiene exists as its dimer, dicyclopentadiene, which has to be 'cracked' by heating it and distilling the monomer (bp 41 °C) in a fractional distillation, collecting it cold. It redimerizes within hours at room temperature, so use it at once.

Dissolve maleic anhydride in ethyl acetate, add ligroin, cool, and add the cyclopentadiene. The reaction is exothermic and the white adduct crystallizes. The product is the endo isomer, cis-norbornene-5,6-endo-dicarboxylic anhydride (mp 164–165 °C).
The endo isomer is formed faster (kinetic control, through favorable secondary orbital interactions). The exo isomer is more stable, and is formed on heating.
Reflux anthracene and maleic anhydride in xylene (bp about 140 °C) for about 30 minutes. The yellow color of anthracene fades. Cool, filter and wash. The adduct melts at about 262 °C.
The diene is the central ring of anthracene, which loses little aromatic stabilization because the two outer rings stay aromatic.
IR: the cyclic anhydride shows two C=O bands, about 1860 and 1780 cm⁻¹.
NMR distinguishes endo from exo, from the coupling and chemical shifts of the bridgehead and alkene protons.

sections.text: Maleic anhydride hydrolyzes in water to maleic acid, so use dry glassware and solvents. It is a skin and respiratory irritant.

quiz.q: Why must cyclopentadiene be freshly cracked before use?
quiz.a: It dimerizes to dicyclopentadiene at room temperature
wrong: It is a gas at room temperature

quiz.q: How many C=O bands does a cyclic anhydride show in IR?
quiz.a: Two

entries.name: Experiment: nitration of methyl benzoate
entries.tagline: Electrophilic aromatic substitution on a deactivated ring: the meta product.

sections.text: Sulfuric acid makes the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, the electrophile. The ester is electron-withdrawing, so the ring is deactivated and the attack goes meta.

points: Cool methyl benzoate in concentrated H₂SO₄ in an ice bath to below 10 °C. Separately cool a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.
Add the nitrating mixture dropwise with stirring, keeping the temperature at 5–15 °C. The reaction is strongly exothermic. A higher temperature gives more of the ortho isomer and dinitration.
After a few minutes at room temperature, pour onto crushed ice. The product precipitates.
Filter by vacuum, wash with cold water and a little cold methanol, and recrystallize from methanol or methanol–water. The melting point of methyl 3-nitrobenzoate is 78 °C. Typical yield: 60–80%.
A melting point below 78 °C and a broad range suggest the ortho isomer (mp about 42 °C) or leftover starting material.
IR: asymmetric and symmetric NO₂ stretches at about 1530 and 1350 cm⁻¹, ester C=O near 1720.
¹H NMR: four distinct aromatic signals for the 1,3-disubstituted ring, near 8.8 (singlet-like), 8.4, 8.3 and 7.6 ppm (triplet), and a methyl singlet near 3.95 ppm.

sections.text: Concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids are very corrosive and oxidizing. Work in a hood and add the mixture slowly. Brown NO₂ gas indicates over-heating.

quiz.q: Why does nitration of methyl benzoate give the meta product?
quiz.a: The ester group is deactivating and meta-directing
wrong: The ester is an activating group

entries.name: Experiment: Friedel–Crafts acylation
entries.tagline: Putting an acyl group on a ring, with a strong Lewis acid or a mild one.

points: Anhydrous aluminium chloride reacts violently with water, so use dry glassware, a drying tube, and a trap for the HCl gas that is given off.
Add acetyl chloride to AlCl₃ in dichloromethane at 0 °C, then toluene dropwise. A full equivalent of AlCl₃ is needed, because the product ketone binds to it.

Quench by pouring slowly onto ice and concentrated HCl to break the complex, extract, wash with bicarbonate, dry and evaporate. The product, 4-methylacetophenone, is mostly para, because methyl directs ortho and para and the para position is less hindered. The acyl group deactivates the ring, so only one adds.
Ferrocene is very electron-rich and reacts with acetic anhydride and phosphoric acid, with no AlCl₃. Heat gently, pour onto ice, neutralize with sodium bicarbonate, and filter.

Separate the products by column chromatography or TLC. The order of elution on silica is ferrocene (yellow, least polar, first), then acetylferrocene (orange, mp 85 °C) and then diacetylferrocene (red).
Ferrocene itself melts at 173 °C.

sections.text: IR: a ketone C=O stretch near 1680 cm⁻¹ (conjugated with the ring). NMR of 4-methylacetophenone: two doublets in the aromatic region (para-substituted, 7.9 and 7.3 ppm), and two methyl singlets (2.57 and 2.42 ppm).

quiz.q: Why is a full equivalent of AlCl₃ needed in Friedel–Crafts acylation?
quiz.a: The product ketone forms a complex with it
wrong: AlCl₃ is consumed to make HCl only

entries.name: Experiment: oxidation and reduction (camphor, borneol, cyclohexanol)
entries.tagline: A green oxidation with household bleach, and a stereoselective reduction.

points: Cyclohexanol or borneol/isoborneol is stirred with acetic acid and sodium hypochlorite solution (bleach). The acid makes hypochlorous acid, the oxidant. This replaces chromium(VI) reagents, which are toxic.
Check for excess oxidant with starch–iodide paper (it turns blue-black), and destroy it with sodium bisulfite. Extract, wash with bicarbonate, dry, and evaporate to give cyclohexanone or camphor.
IR: the O–H band (3300) disappears and a C=O band appears (cyclohexanone 1715 cm⁻¹, camphor 1740, which is high because of the strained ring).

sections.h: Reduction of camphor with sodium borohydride
points: Sodium borohydride is added in portions to camphor in methanol, and the mixture is heated gently. Add water to precipitate the product.

Hydride attacks from the less hindered side of the carbonyl, which is opposite the bulky bridge methyl group, giving mostly isoborneol (about 85%). The ratio of the two diastereomers is a measure of the stereoselectivity.
GC or ¹H NMR gives the ratio: the CH–OH signals are at about 3.6 ppm (isoborneol) and 4.0 ppm (borneol).
Melting points: borneol about 208 °C, isoborneol about 212 °C, in a sealed tube since they sublime.

sections.text: One mole of NaBH₄ can reduce four moles of ketone. It reacts slowly with methanol, so an excess is used. In both experiments the change in IR (loss or gain of C=O) is the clearest evidence.

quiz.q: Which diastereomer is the major product of reducing camphor with NaBH₄?
quiz.a: Isoborneol

quiz.q: How can excess hypochlorite oxidant be detected?
quiz.a: Starch–iodide paper turns blue-black

entries.name: Experiment: Wittig reaction (stilbene)
entries.tagline: Forming a C=C bond at exactly the right place.

equations: Ph₃P⁺–CH₂Ph Cl⁻ + PhCHO + NaOH → PhCH=CHPh + Ph₃P=O + NaCl + H₂O
sections.text: Hydroxide deprotonates the phosphonium salt to give the ylide, which attacks benzaldehyde. The resulting oxaphosphetane collapses to the alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide.

points: A two-phase version: benzyltriphenylphosphonium chloride and benzaldehyde in dichloromethane are stirred vigorously with 50% aqueous sodium hydroxide for about 30 minutes. The ylide forms at the interface and is orange.
Separate the organic layer, wash with water and bisulfite (to remove unreacted benzaldehyde) and brine, dry and evaporate.
The product is a mixture of cis- and trans-stilbene. Heating it with a trace of iodine in light converts the cis into the more stable trans isomer.
Purify by recrystallization from ethanol, which leaves most of the triphenylphosphine oxide in solution. trans-Stilbene melts at 124 °C, while cis-stilbene is a liquid (mp 5 °C).
¹H NMR: the trans alkene protons are a singlet near 7.1 ppm (equivalent by symmetry), and the cis near 6.6 ppm. In unsymmetrical alkenes the coupling is 12–18 Hz for trans and 6–12 Hz for cis.
TLC shows trans-stilbene (higher Rf than the phosphine oxide, which is polar).
A mixed melting point or GC gives purity and the cis/trans ratio.

sections.text: A semistabilized ylide such as the benzyl ylide gives a mixture of E and Z. Triphenylphosphine oxide is the thermodynamic driving force and the main waste, giving a poor atom economy.

quiz.q: What drives the Wittig reaction thermodynamically?
quiz.a: Formation of the strong P=O bond in triphenylphosphine oxide

entries.name: Experiment: aspirin and Williamson ether synthesis
entries.tagline: Making a familiar drug by acylation, and an ether by SN2.

equations: salicylic acid + (CH₃CO)₂O → acetylsalicylic acid + CH₃COOH    (H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄ catalyst)
points: Warm salicylic acid with acetic anhydride and a few drops of phosphoric or sulfuric acid at about 50–60 °C for 10–15 minutes.
Add water cautiously to destroy the excess anhydride. Cool in ice to crystallize, filter, and wash with cold water.
Recrystallize from ethanol and water (aspirin mp about 135 °C).
Purity test: ferric chloride gives a purple color with the phenol of unreacted salicylic acid, but not with pure aspirin. Compare the product with salicylic acid and a commercial tablet.
Typical yield: 60–80%. The product smells of vinegar if it is wet, since aspirin hydrolyzes slowly.

Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is deprotonated at the phenol with potassium carbonate, and the phenoxide attacks iodoethane (SN2) in refluxing butanone or acetone, giving 4-ethoxyacetanilide (phenacetin, mp 134–136 °C).
The nucleophile is the phenoxide O, since it is more acidic than the amide N–H, and the halide must be primary to avoid elimination.
Workup: filter off the salts, remove the solvent, partition between water and dichloromethane, wash with base, dry and recrystallize.
Phenacetin was once an analgesic but was withdrawn because of kidney toxicity.

sections.text: IR of aspirin shows two C=O bands (acid at about 1690 and ester at 1750 cm⁻¹). For the ether, the phenol O–H is gone, and NMR shows an ethoxy group (a quartet at 4.0 and a triplet at 1.4 ppm).

quiz.q: How does the ferric chloride test show whether aspirin is pure?
quiz.a: Unreacted salicylic acid, a phenol, gives a purple color
wrong: Pure aspirin gives a purple color
It turns red with the ester
It forms a precipitate with aspirin

entries.name: Experiment: isolating natural products (caffeine, limonene, eugenol)
entries.tagline: Extraction and steam distillation applied to tea, oranges and cloves.

points: Boil tea leaves in water with sodium carbonate. Caffeine dissolves, and the base converts the tannins (acidic phenols) into water-soluble salts so they stay in the water layer, and keeps caffeine as the free base.

Extract the cooled solution with dichloromethane several times, since caffeine is about nine times more soluble in dichloromethane than in water. Vigorous shaking causes emulsions, so swirl gently, add brine, or filter.
Dry the dichloromethane, evaporate, and purify the crude by recrystallization or sublimation. Caffeine melts at 235–238 °C and sublimes near 178 °C.
Analysis: TLC against a standard, melting point, and IR (two C=O bands, no O–H).
Grated orange peel is steam distilled. The distillate has an oily layer of limonene (bp 176 °C) on water, which is extracted into dichloromethane, dried and evaporated.

Limonene is chiral. The (R)-(+) enantiomer is the one in oranges, and it smells of orange. Optical rotation in a polarimeter confirms it (specific rotation about +115° to +125° for the pure compound).

Steam distill ground cloves, extract the distillate with dichloromethane, and separate the phenol (eugenol) from neutral compounds (eugenyl acetate, caryophyllene) by extracting with aqueous NaOH, which makes the phenolate. Acidify the water layer to recover eugenol, and extract it again.
Eugenol boils at 254 °C and smells of cloves. IR: a broad O–H band and an allyl C=C.

sections.text: These show the use of acid–base chemistry and polarity in separations, and the partition coefficient: a compound distributes between two liquids in a fixed ratio, so several small extractions are more efficient than one large one.

quiz.q: Why is sodium carbonate added when extracting caffeine from tea?
quiz.a: It makes tannins water-soluble so they stay out of the organic layer

quiz.q: Why is steam distillation used for limonene?
quiz.a: Limonene is immiscible with water and distills below 100 °C with it
wrong: It is faster than any other method

entries.name: Experiment: azo dye synthesis (methyl orange)
entries.tagline: Diazotization followed by azo coupling, and a dye that is also an indicator.

equations: sulfanilic acid + NaNO₂ + HCl (0–5 °C) → diazonium salt
diazonium + PhNMe₂ (acetic acid), then NaOH → methyl orange

points: Dissolve sulfanilic acid in aqueous sodium carbonate (it is a zwitterion and is soluble as the sodium salt), add sodium nitrite, and pour the solution into ice and hydrochloric acid at 0–5 °C. The diazonium salt (as a zwitterion) separates as a fine solid.
Test for a slight excess of nitrous acid with starch–iodide paper (blue-black).
Add N,N-dimethylaniline in acetic acid. The coupling goes at the para position of the aniline. A red solid (the acid form) appears.
Make basic with NaOH, which turns the dye orange (the sodium salt). Heat, add sodium chloride to salt it out, cool, and filter. Recrystallize from hot water.

Methyl orange is an acid–base indicator: red below pH 3.1 and yellow-orange above pH 4.4. The color change is due to protonation of the azo group, which changes the conjugation. Its absorption maximum in base is about 464 nm.
Diazonium salts are unstable above about 5 °C and explosive when dry, so keep them cold and use them wet.
Aromatic azo compounds are highly colored because of the extended conjugation across –N=N–.

quiz.q: Why is diazotization carried out at 0–5 °C?
quiz.a: Diazonium salts decompose at higher temperatures
wrong: Sulfanilic acid is insoluble in the cold

entries.name: Experiment: Suzuki coupling and green chemistry
entries.tagline: A palladium-catalyzed biaryl synthesis done in water and ethanol.

sections.text: The reaction is a Suzuki cross-coupling. The catalytic cycle: oxidative addition of the aryl bromide to Pd(0), transmetalation from the boronate (formed by base), and reductive elimination of the biaryl.

points: Combine the aryl bromide, phenylboronic acid (a slight excess), a base such as sodium or potassium carbonate, a very small amount of palladium acetate (often under 1 mol%) and the water–ethanol solvent. Heat at 60–80 °C for 15–60 minutes.
The mixture darkens. A black precipitate of palladium metal ('Pd black') at the end shows the catalyst has decomposed.
Cool, add water, and filter the solid or extract with ethyl acetate. Purify by recrystallization or a short column. 4-Methoxybiphenyl melts at about 90 °C.
Monitor by TLC: the biaryl is less polar than boronic acid and is UV-active.
Water and ethanol as the solvent instead of toluene or DMF.
A very small amount of catalyst, and mild conditions.
Boronic acids and the boric acid by-product are low in toxicity.
Atom economy is moderate, since the halide and the boron group are lost. The E-factor is a way to compare the waste per kilogram of product.

quiz.q: What does a black precipitate at the end of a Suzuki reaction usually indicate?
quiz.a: The palladium catalyst has decomposed to palladium metal
wrong: The reaction has gone to completion

entries.name: Experiment: qualitative organic analysis and functional group tests
entries.tagline: Identifying an unknown compound from solubility, chemical tests, derivatives and spectra.

sections.text: Test the unknown in water, ether, 5% NaOH, 5% NaHCO₃, 5% HCl and concentrated H₂SO₄. A carboxylic acid dissolves in both NaOH and NaHCO₃. A phenol dissolves in NaOH only. An amine dissolves in HCl. A neutral compound with oxygen dissolves in cold concentrated sulfuric acid. A hydrocarbon or alkyl halide does not dissolve in any of these.

facts: Yellow precipitate of CHI₃: methyl ketones and ethanol or secondary alcohols with a CH₃CH(OH)– group.
Orange to green within seconds: primary and secondary alcohols and aldehydes. Tertiary alcohols do not react.
Purple, blue or green: phenols and enols.
A precipitate: alkyl halides (rate shows the class).

sections.text: To confirm an identity, convert the unknown into a solid derivative with a sharp melting point and compare it with tables: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones or semicarbazones of aldehydes and ketones, 3,5-dinitrobenzoates of alcohols, and amides or anilides of acids.

In practice an unknown is identified by combining the physical constants (boiling or melting point), the tests above, IR (functional groups), mass spectrum (molecular mass), and ¹H and ¹³C NMR. The chemical tests are useful as quick confirmations and teach the reactivity of the groups.

quiz.q: A compound gives a yellow-orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP and a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. What is it?
quiz.a: An aldehyde

quiz.q: Which compound dissolves in both NaOH and NaHCO₃?
quiz.a: A carboxylic acid

entries.name: Experiment: making polymers (the nylon rope trick)
entries.tagline: A condensation polymer drawn out of a beaker as a continuous rope.

points: A solution of sebacoyl chloride (a diacid chloride) in hexane or dichloromethane is carefully layered on top of an aqueous solution of hexamethylenediamine containing sodium hydroxide.
The polymer forms as a film at the boundary between the two layers, where the monomers meet. It is lifted out with tweezers and wound onto a rod as a rope, and a new film forms as it is removed.
The sodium hydroxide neutralizes the HCl that is released, which would otherwise protonate the diamine and stop the reaction.
Wash the nylon thoroughly with water and ethanol before touching, because the acid chloride is corrosive and irritating.

sections.text: A step-growth (condensation) polymerization between a diacid chloride and a diamine gives a polyamide. This is nylon-6,10 (the numbers are the carbons in the diamine and in the diacid). Nylon-6,6 is made from hexanedioyl (adipoyl) chloride, and it is usually made industrially from the diacid and diamine.

points: Radical polymerization of styrene or methyl methacrylate with an initiator such as AIBN or benzoyl peroxide, to make polystyrene or PMMA. The initiator breaks into radicals on heating.
Polyesters from a diacid and a diol, with an acid catalyst and removal of water.
Properties are tested by solubility, melting range, and density, and viscosity gives the molar mass.

quiz.q: Why is NaOH in the aqueous layer in the nylon rope trick?
quiz.a: It neutralizes the HCl released so the diamine stays reactive
wrong: It catalyzes the formation of the rope

entries.name: Physical constants: polarimetry and refractive index
entries.tagline: Two quick measurements that identify a liquid and show the optical purity of a chiral compound.

sections.text: Plane-polarized light is rotated when it passes through a solution of a chiral compound. α is the measured rotation in degrees, l the path length in decimeters and c the concentration in g/mL. The specific rotation [α] is quoted at a temperature and wavelength, usually the sodium D line (589 nm), for example [α]²⁰_D. Dextrorotatory (+) is clockwise and levorotatory (−) is counterclockwise. The sign does not tell you R or S.

points: Optical purity (%) = [α]_observed ÷ [α]_pure × 100, which equals the enantiomeric excess if the relationship is linear.
Sucrose is +66.5° and is a classic example. Racemic mixtures show no rotation.
The measurement is sensitive to concentration, solvent, temperature and impurities.
An Abbe refractometer measures how much light bends in a liquid, from the critical angle, with a few drops of sample. n_D²⁰ is measured at 20 °C with the D line.
The index falls by about 0.0004 per °C, so correct to a reference temperature.
Typical values: water 1.3330, hexane 1.3751, ethyl acetate 1.3723, cyclohexane 1.4262, cyclohexene 1.4465, toluene 1.4969.
Comparing the index of a distilled product with the literature value is a quick purity check.

quiz.q: What does a specific rotation of 0° for a chiral compound suggest?
quiz.a: It may be a racemic mixture
wrong: It is pure and enantiomerically pure
